what: Verification that the containerised Model 1 v2 service reproduces the committed native results.

image.note: torch is installed from PyTorch's CPU index at the version requirements-serving.txt pins. The default Linux wheel bundles the CUDA runtime, which this service can never use, and cost 2.8 GB. Switching indexes left every prediction byte-identical; see accuracy.cpu_wheel_equivalence.
image.checkpoints_note: Mounted read-only at run time. Not baked into any layer.

checkpoint_verification.method: sha256 of each mounted file compared with armor-system/models/model1_transformer/results/test_freeze/evidence_test_freeze.json
checkpoint_verification.note: The service also reports these over /v1/metadata, so a running container proves which weights it loaded.

accuracy.method: replay_demo.py streamed 875 recorded D1 validation minutes through the container's HTTP API

cpu_wheel_equivalence.claim: Switching torch from the CUDA-bundled wheel to the CPU wheel changed no prediction.
cpu_wheel_equivalence.evidence: incidents.jsonl from the two replay runs is byte-identical, and every non-timing field of replay_summary.json is equal.

latency.method: bench.py run inside the container, same script and synthetic inputs as the native run
latency.finding: Per-window server time is six to ten times the native reference (68-99 ms against 8-10 ms). The two runs differ in both CPU and virtualisation, so this does not isolate container overhead from the hardware difference; it is an upper bound for this host. The CPU wheel is indistinguishable from the CUDA-bundled wheel on compute and loads faster, 2.7 s against 6.7 s, because there is far less to read. Still far inside budget: the service is called once a minute, so ~99 ms of a 60000 ms budget, under 0.2%.

conclusion: Containerised results are identical to the committed native results, and remain identical after slimming the image tenfold. Only latency differs, and it stays well inside the per-minute budget.
